newsitem.title: UK: Commodity markets rangebound despite wider U.S. trade gap.
newsitem.headline: Commodity markets rangebound despite wider U.S. trade gap.

text.p: Most commodity markets remained rangebound on Wedndesday despite the U.S. trade gap saoring to its widest in eight years and provoking falls in the dollar and stock markets.
Gold attracted little "safe haven" buying as the financial markets lost value.

Dealers said bullion continued to await news of whether or not the International Monetary Fund (IMF) would agree to sell about five million ounces of its 104 million-ounce gold reserve to realise funds to help the world's poorest nations.
A decision was possible late on Wednesday.
Copper prices rose on the London Metal Exchange (LME) and appeared to be sustaining their rally above the psychological $1,900-a-tonne level, traders said.
Three month copper futures finished the afternoon session at $1,925, up $55 from Tuesday's afternoon kerb close.
The market started to rally late on Tuesday, led by buying and investment bank interest on New York's Comex futures market.

Physical traders said demand for LME copper in Europe had picked up recently, reflecting shipments to the Far East and merchant stockbuilding. "People are now prepared to take stock positions," said one physical copper merchant.
Other base metals followed copper's lead with aluminium finishing $16.50 higher at $1,433.
White sugar futures rose after Tuesday's fall but traders were sceptical about the likely strength of the move.
"We are seeing a bounce following the trade and investment fund selling that sent the market reeling on Tuesday...its technically correcting," one trader said.
Robusta coffee futures traded higher early but turned around to post losses later as the reaction to the recent sell-off ran out of steam.
"People are beginning to feel that perhaps the market has seen the worst of the initial sell-off and perhaps that we will have a little more sideways movement," one trader said.

Part of coffee's weakness came from news major producer Brazil had scrapped a 13-percent export tax recently leading the market to anticipate a flood of Brazilian exports with consequently lower prices.
Cocoa pricers moved sideways as well. "There's nothing to interest anybody at the moment," said a trader. "The crop news is all out. There's nothing for the market to trade on.
There was no price reaction to Malaysia's major cocoa planter Golden Hope Plantations saying it would quit cocoa growing by June 1999 due to prolonged weak cocoa prices.

The U.S. grain fututes markets were generally lower in thin volume. "Tomorrow (Thursday) is the last trading day and it's so thin that just a little selling takes it down," said a trader in the Chicago Board of Trade corn futures pit.
